title: From Label to Glass
subtitle: How to read a champagne label with confidence, and how to enjoy what is in the bottle once it is open.

episodes.title: What Every Label Must Tell You
episodes.hook: A champagne label can feel like a puzzle written in gold, yet beneath the flourishes it is answering a short list of questions that the law asks of every bottle. Once you know those questions, any label becomes easy to read.
cards: A champagne label can look like a small work of art, all foil and flourishes, but beneath the decoration it is also a legal document with a job to do.
French and European rules decide what must appear on it, and France's consumer protection office, the DGCCRF, publishes a plain guide to reading a champagne label.
The first thing the rules ask for is the word Champagne itself, printed in characters that are clearly visible on the label.
That same word must be repeated on the part of the cork that sits inside the neck, so you can check it once more after the bottle is open.
For the smallest bottles, those of twenty centilitres or less, the word may appear on another inner part of the closure instead of the cork.
Most French appellation wines also carry the phrase appellation d'origine contrôlée, but champagne is not required to, because the single word Champagne already carries that meaning.
The Union des Maisons de Champagne, the association of the houses, explains that every champagne is by definition an appellation wine, so the longer phrase was never demanded of it.
Next comes a word for sweetness, chosen from a short official list that runs from brut nature to doux. Those words, and their curious order, have the next episode to themselves.
The label must also name the élaborateur, the producer responsible for making the wine, along with the commune, meaning the town or village, where that producer is based.
Beside it sits a registration number issued by the Comité Champagne, the interprofessional body that brings the region's growers and houses together.
That number is preceded by two small initials, such as NM or RM, which tell you what kind of producer made the wine. They too have an episode of their own.
Then come the vitals you will find on almost any bottle of wine in Europe: the alcoholic strength, given as a percentage by volume, and the volume the bottle holds.
There is also a lot number, which lets a producer trace a batch, a mention of allergens such as sulphites, and a health message or symbol for pregnant women.
Wines made since 8 December 2023 must also give an ingredients list and nutrition details under European rules, though much of this may sit behind a QR code.
Many other words are optional, such as a vintage year, blanc de blancs or blanc de noirs, or the name of a village. When they do appear, they come with rules of their own.
Grand cru and premier cru are among those optional words. In Champagne they rank whole villages, and grand cru may be used only when every grape grew in the seventeen top villages.
French bottles once wore a small tax seal on the capsule, known as the CRD. The DGCCRF notes that it has not been compulsory since 1 June 2019.
So the compulsory words are few, and none of them tells you whether a wine is good. What they promise instead is honesty about what it is and who stands behind it.
That is a quiet comfort in front of a crowded shelf. Once you know where to look, every bottle answers the same handful of questions in the same plain way.
episodes.setup: Of all the words the rules ask for, one is both the most useful and the most puzzling. Why would a wine called extra dry taste sweeter than one called brut?

episodes.title: The Words for Sweetness
episodes.hook: Nearly every champagne carries a word that tells you how sweet it is, and the words follow an order that can seem back to front. Their story begins in a century when champagne was far sweeter than it is today.
episodes.callback: We found the handful of things every champagne label must tell you, from the cork in the neck to the small print.
cards: Almost every champagne is finished with a small addition called the dosage, given just after the yeast sediment is removed from the bottle in a step called dégorgement.
The dosage is made with a liqueur d'expédition, a mixture of wine and sugar, and the amount a producer adds largely sets how dry or how sweet the finished wine will taste.
Because the dosage is a choice, the label must say where the result sits, using one of seven terms laid down in European regulations.
At the driest end is brut nature, for wines with less than three grams of sugar per litre, and only when no sugar at all was added after the second fermentation.
You may also see that idea written as pas dosé or dosage zéro, gentle ways of saying that the wine was given no dosage at all.
Next comes extra brut, for wines with between nought and six grams of sugar per litre, followed by brut, for wines with less than twelve grams.
Brut is the word you are most likely to have met at a wedding or a celebration, because it appears on a great many of the champagnes you will find on any shelf.
Then the scale turns sweeter. Extra dry covers twelve to seventeen grams per litre, sec covers seventeen to thirty-two, and demi-sec covers thirty-two to fifty.
At the far end stands doux, for wines with more than fifty grams of sugar per litre. It is rarely made today, though very sweet champagne was once widely enjoyed.
The bands meet and overlap at their edges, so a wine with four grams could honestly be called brut or extra brut. The rules ask the producer to choose only one.
The rules also allow a little leeway, because the real sugar content may differ from what the label implies by no more than three grams per litre.
So the order is clear, from brut nature to doux, and it is perfectly natural to wonder why extra dry should sit on the sweeter side of brut.
The usual explanation is that these words were coined at different times, when the champagne they described was much sweeter than the champagne most of us drink now.

In the nineteenth century a great deal of champagne was very sweet indeed, and sources describe the Russian market taking wines several times sweeter than the fifty grams per litre where doux begins today.
British drinkers are generally credited with leading the move towards drier wines, and in that world a wine called dry was dry only by the standards of its own day.
A well-known story says that Perrier-Jouët left its 1846 wine unsweetened for London, though careful histories treat that tale as partly legend.
Pommery is usually credited with an early brut from the 1874 harvest, a story told largely by the house itself and best enjoyed in that spirit.
In the usual account, brut arrived later as a newer and drier word, while the older words, sec and extra dry among them, kept describing sweeter wines.
We cannot point to a single document that settled the order, but the explanation fits what is known: each word keeps the taste of the time when it seemed right.
When you choose a bottle, then, trust the word rather than the feeling it gives you. An extra dry or a sec is simply a softer, rounder style, and it can be a real pleasure.
episodes.setup: Beside the sweetness word sit two tiny letters and a number. They are easy to overlook, and they tell you who actually made the wine.

episodes.title: The Small Letters Beside the Number
episodes.hook: Somewhere on every champagne label, often in tiny print, two letters sit beside a number. They are easy to miss, yet they tell you something that no amount of gold foil can: what kind of producer actually made the wine.
episodes.callback: We traced the sweetness words from brut nature to doux, and saw why extra dry sits on the sweeter side of brut.
cards: The two letters come just before the registration number issued by the Comité Champagne, and French guidance explains that they show the producer's professional category.
They matter because a handsome brand name could belong to almost anyone, while the letters tell you how the grapes and the winemaking came together.
NM stands for négociant-manipulant. A négociant is a merchant and a manipulant is one who makes the wine, so this is a house that may buy grapes and makes wine under its own name.
Many houses farm vineyards of their own as well, so NM does not mean that a house grows nothing. It means that buying from others is open to it, and part of how many houses work.
Most of the famous names you meet on restaurant lists carry NM, and it was the great houses that carried the reputation of champagne around the world.
RM stands for récoltant-manipulant. A récoltant is a harvester, so this is a grower who makes and sells champagne from grapes they have grown themselves.
These wines are often called grower champagne, and many drinkers seek them out because a grower's wine can reflect a single village, or even a single slope.
CM stands for coopérative de manipulation, a cooperative of growers that pools its members' grapes, makes the wine together, and sells it under one or more brands of its own.
Cooperatives are an important part of Champagne, because they give growers a shared press house and cellar without each family having to build its own.
RC stands for récoltant-coopérateur. Here a grower's grapes are made into wine at the cooperative, and the grower takes back finished bottles to sell under the family's own name.
This is the code most worth reading twice, because an RC bottle can look just like a grower's own wine, even though the wine was made in a shared cellar.
SR stands for société de récoltants, a company formed by growers, often from one family, who make and sell their champagne together. Sources describe it as rare.
ND stands for négociant-distributeur, a business that buys finished bottles from someone else and sells them under its own name, without having made the wine itself.
MA stands for marque d'acheteur, which means the buyer's own brand. A supermarket, restaurant or wine merchant can own the name on the front while another producer makes the wine.
A buyer's own brand can be perfectly sound wine, and it is always worth turning the bottle to see whether the back label also names the producer who made it.
So none of these codes is a grade. A house marked NM can make some of the region's most profound wines, and a grower marked RM can make an ordinary one.
What the letters give you instead is a good question to carry into the shop: did the people who grew these grapes also make this wine, and if not, who did?
Once you begin to notice them, the two small letters become one of the most interesting things on a label, a short history of the bottle in your hand.
episodes.setup: The two letters tell you who made the wine. Next we ask what a year on the label promises, and why most bottles choose to carry none.

episodes.title: What the Year on the Label Promises
episodes.hook: A year on a champagne label is a promise that the grapes came from a single harvest, and most bottles make no such promise at all. The reasons say a great deal about how champagne is made, and about what its makers value.
episodes.callback: We read the two small letters that tell you who made the wine, from NM and RM all the way to MA.
cards: In Champagne a wine with a year on its label is called millésimé, from millésime, the French word for a vintage, and the year tells you when the grapes were picked.
Across French wine generally, a year on the label requires at least eighty-five per cent of the grapes to come from that harvest, according to the French government's guidance.
Champagne is widely described as stricter still, with every grape in a vintage champagne drawn from the named year, though the sources we found for this were secondary.
Most champagne, however, carries no year at all, and you will often see it called non-vintage, sometimes shortened to NV.
A non-vintage champagne is usually a blend from several harvests, an assemblage built around one main year and supported by older wines kept for the purpose.
Those older wines are called reserve wines. They are held back from earlier harvests so that a house or grower can soften the differences between one year and the next.
In a northern region where the weather can vary greatly, blending across years lets a producer offer a familiar style even after a difficult harvest.
So a missing year is no sign of a lesser wine. It reflects a choice to value consistency, and many producers think of their non-vintage blend as their signature.
Making a vintage champagne is a choice as well, and no official body tells a producer when to do it. Most keep it for years they feel deserve to stand alone.
The rules also set minimum ageing times, counted from the tirage, the moment when the wine is bottled with yeast and sugar to begin its second fermentation in the bottle.
During that time the wine rests on its lees, the spent yeast, which slowly break down in a process called autolysis and bring flavours often likened to bread or brioche.
Champagne's rules say that the wine may not be disgorged, meaning cleared of its yeast sediment, until at least twelve months after the tirage.
A non-vintage champagne may not be sold to consumers until at least fifteen months after the tirage, so it will have spent at least twelve of those months on its lees.
A vintage champagne must wait longer, at least thirty-six months from the tirage, which is three full years in the cellar before it may be released.
These are only minimums, and many producers choose to wait much longer, because patient time on the lees is one of the ways champagne gains depth.
Some back labels now share more of the story, giving the date of disgorgement or the base year of a non-vintage blend, which helps you guess how fresh or mature it may taste.
Neither kind of champagne is simply better than the other. A vintage shows you the character of one year, while a non-vintage shows you the craft of blending several.
So when you see a year, read it as a portrait of one harvest, and when you see none, read it as a producer's chosen voice, carried carefully from year to year.
episodes.setup: A year on the label is one kind of promise. The size of the bottle carries another, and the names of the largest sizes come from a surprising place.

episodes.title: Bottle Sizes and Their Names
episodes.hook: Champagne comes in a remarkable range of sizes, from a small bottle meant for one to giants that need both hands to pour. Many of the largest carry names borrowed from the Bible, and nobody is quite sure why.
episodes.callback: We saw what a year on the label promises, and why most champagne prefers to carry none.
cards: The Comité Champagne's education materials list the sizes in order, and the smallest is the quart, a quarter bottle that holds twenty centilitres.
Next comes the demie, a half bottle of thirty-seven and a half centilitres, and then the familiar standard bottle, which holds seventy-five centilitres.
The magnum holds one and a half litres, the equal of two standard bottles. Its name comes from a Latin word meaning great, and it is not one of the biblical names.
From there the names grow grander. The jéroboam, or jeroboam in English, holds three litres, and the réhoboam holds four and a half.
The mathusalem, or methuselah, holds six litres, the salmanazar nine, the balthazar twelve, and the nabuchodonosor, which English speakers call the nebuchadnezzar, fifteen.
The list continues with the salomon at eighteen litres, then the very rare souverain and primat, and finally the melchisédech, which holds thirty litres.
A few of these names mean different sizes in other regions. In Bordeaux, for example, a jeroboam is not the three-litre bottle that the name describes in Champagne.
Most of the names belong to figures from the Bible, kings and patriarchs among them, and Methuselah is the patriarch whom Genesis describes as living longest of all.
Why biblical names were chosen at all is genuinely unclear. The Comité Champagne's own website says that historians have not been able to find an explanation.
Some writers suggest the jeroboam came first and the other names followed in its spirit, perhaps half in jest, but this remains a suggestion rather than a documented history.
So we will not offer a tidy origin story here. The names are a pleasure to say, and their beginnings simply have not been traced with any certainty.
Size matters to the wine as well as to the party. Champagne's rules say that champagne is sold in the bottle in which its second fermentation took place.
That rule has exceptions at the edges. The quarter bottle and the large formats, from the jeroboam upward, may be filled by transferring wine under pressure from other bottles.
The standard bottle and the magnum, by contrast, must hold the very wine that fermented and aged inside them, which is part of the magnum's quiet appeal.
It is often said that champagne matures more slowly and gracefully in a magnum than in a standard bottle, though that comes from experience and opinion rather than from the rules.
The very largest bottles are made mostly for celebrations and rare occasions, and pouring from one is as much a ceremony as a service.
For everyday pleasure the standard bottle remains the friendliest companion, and a magnum makes a generous choice whenever friends gather.
Whatever the size, the same labelling rules apply, so the word Champagne, the sweetness term and the two small letters are always there to guide you.
episodes.setup: Once a bottle is open, which glass should it go into? The answer begins with a famous legend about a queen of France.

episodes.title: Flute, Coupe or Wine Glass
episodes.hook: For a long time the choice seemed simple: a tall flute for weddings, or a wide coupe for something more glamorous. Today many people in Champagne would gently suggest a third shape, and their reasons are well worth hearing.
episodes.callback: We climbed the bottle sizes from the quart to the melchisédech, and found that nobody knows quite why they wear biblical names.
cards: The coupe is the wide, shallow glass on a stem that you may picture at a grand old party, with towers of glasses filled from the very top.
A much-loved story says its shape was modelled on the breast of Marie Antoinette, the queen of France who died in 1793, and it is easy to see why the tale has lasted.
It joins a famous queen to a glamorous glass, and hints at a lost world of court parties at Versailles, which makes it a very pleasing story to repeat.
There is even a real object behind the legend. The Sèvres porcelain works made breast-shaped bowls for the queen's dairy at Rambouillet, delivered in 1788.
Those were porcelain bowls for a dairy, however, rather than champagne glasses, and there is no evidence that the coupe was copied from the queen.
Shallow glasses of this kind are generally dated to long before her lifetime, and the same story has been told of other women, including Madame de Pompadour and the Empress Joséphine.
So the coupe has a charming legend rather than a royal model, and it still has its place whenever the look of a glass matters as much as the wine within it.
Its wide, open bowl lets the aromas drift away quickly, and many writers note that the bubbles fade sooner in a coupe than in a narrower glass.
The tall, narrow flute is the familiar alternative, and its slender shape gives the bubbles a long path to rise in a fine, steady line.
Scientists at the University of Reims, measuring the gas just above poured champagne, found the carbon dioxide concentration significantly higher above a flute than above a coupe.
That gas can prickle the nose, which is one reason some tasters feel that a flute shows off the bubbles while crowding the wine's aromas.
The Comité Champagne now suggests that neither shape suits champagne best. Its advice is a tall glass with a rounded bowl that narrows towards the top, shaped like a tulip.
In a tulip glass the wider middle gives the aromas room to gather, while the narrower rim guides them towards you and helps the bubbles last.
Many sommeliers and producers go a step further and happily serve champagne in a good white wine glass, which has much the same gentle shape.
The case for a tulip or a wine glass rests largely on tasting experience, because the careful measurements so far concern the gas above the glass rather than how aromas are perceived.
How you pour matters too. Researchers have reported that pouring down the side of a tilted glass keeps much more of the dissolved gas than pouring straight down the middle.
A clean glass helps as well, since traces of detergent can affect the bubbles, which is why many people rinse their champagne glasses thoroughly in hot water.
In the end the best glass is the one that lets you enjoy the wine. A flute for a toast, a coupe for nostalgia and a tulip for close attention can share one happy evening.
episodes.setup: From the glass we move to the rest of the table, where the pop, the sabre and the silver spoon each have a story waiting.

episodes.title: Myths at the Table
episodes.hook: Champagne gathers little rituals around it: the loud pop, the dramatic sabre, the silver spoon slipped into an unfinished bottle. Some of them help, some do no harm, and one or two quietly work against the wine.
episodes.callback: We set the coupe's royal legend gently aside and met the tulip glass that the Comité Champagne now recommends.
cards: Begin with temperature. The Comité Champagne's own serving guidance suggests eight to ten degrees Celsius for most champagne, and up to twelve degrees for vintage wines.
When champagne is served much colder than that, its aromas and flavours become harder to notice, which is why an icy glass can seem to taste of very little.
The same guidance suggests a bucket filled with ice and water, rather than ice alone, for around thirty minutes before serving.
Next comes the pop. A sealed bottle of champagne holds its gas at a pressure often given as around six atmospheres, roughly six times the pressure of the air around us.
That is why the loud pop, cheerful as it sounds, is something many in Champagne would rather avoid, because a flying cork can travel fast enough to injure an eye.
Researchers at the University of Reims have measured corks leaving bottles at around forty kilometres per hour at serving temperature, and faster from warmer bottles.
The gentler way is to loosen the wire cage, called the muselet, keep a hand over the cork, and slowly turn the bottle while holding the cork still.
The Union des Maisons de Champagne advises easing the cork out as slowly and gently as possible, so that it leaves with a soft sigh instead of a bang.
A quiet opening also avoids the rush of foam that can follow a sudden pop, so more of the wine, and more of its sparkle, finds its way into your glass.
Sabrage, opening a bottle with a sabre, is the most theatrical ritual of all, and it usually arrives with a story about Napoleon's hussars, the light cavalry, celebrating on horseback.
It is a stirring picture, but careful sources describe the hussar story as a legend, and other tales give the credit to quite different heroes.
When sabrage is done well, the neck of the bottle breaks cleanly away with the cork still inside it. It is a skill that needs training, care and plenty of clear space.
Then there is the spoon. Many families hang a silver teaspoon in the neck of an unfinished bottle, trusting it to keep the bubbles until the next day.
It is easy to see why the habit spread, because a bottle with a spoon often does seem lively the next day, especially when it has spent the night in a cold fridge.
The spoon has been put to the test. In 1994 researchers in Champagne compared open bottles, bottles with a teaspoon in the neck, and properly sealed bottles.
After forty-eight hours, the pressure in the open bottles and in the bottles with a spoon had fallen by a further half, while the sealed bottles were clearly livelier.
A small blind tasting at Stanford University around the same time also found no help from the spoon, so the habit is best kept for its sentiment alone.
What does help is a proper champagne stopper that seals tightly, together with cold, because carbon dioxide dissolves more readily in colder wine.
With a good stopper and a place in the fridge, an opened bottle will usually keep some of its sparkle for a day or two, and some sources suggest several days.
None of this needs to feel like a set of rules. A cool bottle, a gentle opening and a good stopper simply let the wine show you everything it has.
episodes.setup: Last of all, we look back over everything we have read on labels and at the table, and sort what has held up from what we chose to leave out.

episodes.title: Scorecard
episodes.hook: Every thread here ends with an honest account. This is where we gather what has held up, what has changed with the times, which popular versions deserve a gentle correction, and what we chose to leave out, with our reasons.
episodes.callback: We tested the table's rituals, from the quiet opening of a bottle to the silver spoon that does nothing for the bubbles.
cards: First, what has held. The word Champagne on the label and the cork, the sweetness term, and the producer's name, commune and registration remain the heart of every label.
The seven sweetness words and their bands, from brut nature below three grams per litre to doux above fifty, come from European rules and still stand today.
The two small letters still identify the kind of producer behind each bottle, and RC still deserves a second look, since it can resemble a grower's own wine so closely.
The minimum ageing times hold too: fifteen months from the tirage for non-vintage, thirty-six months for vintage, and no disgorging before twelve months have passed.
Next, what has changed. Labels now carry more than they once did, because European rules since December 2023 ask for ingredients and nutrition details, often behind a QR code.
The small tax seal that French bottles once wore on the capsule is no longer compulsory, so its absence on a newer bottle is no cause for worry.
Advice on the glass has moved on as well. In the Comité Champagne's own guidance, the flute and the coupe have given way to a tulip-shaped glass.
Some popular versions deserve a gentle correction. Extra dry being sweeter than brut is not a mistake on the label; it reflects words coined when champagne was sweeter.
The coupe was not modelled on Marie Antoinette, and the silver spoon does not keep the bubbles. In a tested comparison, it did no better than an open bottle.
And a missing year does not mean a lesser wine. Most champagne is blended across harvests by design, to keep a style steady through changing weather.
Finally, what we left out, and why. We have not given firm dates for when the words dry, extra dry and brut first appeared, because sources disagree and some rely on house stories.
We have not offered a single origin for the biblical bottle names, because the Comité Champagne itself says that historians have not found one.
Some sources date the custom of those names to the nineteenth century and others to the twentieth, so we left the date out altogether.
We have not given volumes for every rare giant format, such as the melchior, because the names and sizes differ from one source to another.
We did not say whether a half bottle may be filled by transfer, because the appellation's text and a trade summary describe that exception differently.
We kept a single figure for how long an opened bottle lasts off the cards, because the estimates we found ranged from a day or two to several days.
We have not said who first sabred a bottle, because the hussars, the widow Clicquot and others all have their champions, and none of the stories is documented.
And we have not said what share of champagne is non-vintage, or how much the houses sell compared with the growers, because we could not confirm those figures well enough.
Thank you for reading this far. We hope the next label you hold feels friendly and familiar, and that the bottle behind it tastes all the better for it.
